title-group.article-title: Total neoadjuvant chemotherapy combined with PD‑1 blockade and IL‑2 in MSS/pMMR locally advanced rectal cancer: short-term results of a prospective, single-arm phase II study

abstract.title: Abstract
abstract.p: Neoadjuvant therapy has become a cornerstone in the management of locally advanced rectal cancer (LARC). In this single-arm, open-label phase II study, we evaluated the efficacy and safety of total neoadjuvant chemotherapy (TNT) using a CapOX regimen combined with a programmed cell death protein 1 (PD‑1) antibody (sintilimab) and interleukin‑2 (IL‑2) in patients with microsatellite stable (MSS)/defining proficient mismatch repair (pMMR) LARC. A total of 33 patients, aged 18–75 years, with rectal tumors located within 12 cm from the anal verge and staged as cT3/4N_anyM0 or cT_anyN⁺M0, were enrolled. Patients received a regimen consisting of oxaliplatin, sintilimab, capecitabine, and IL‑2 administered in a three‑week cycle, with response evaluations performed after every two cycles. Following six cycles of treatment, 33 patients underwent radical surgery, achieving a 100% R0 resection rate. The pathological complete response (pCR) rate was 42.4% (95% CI: 25.68–59.16%) while the remaining 19 patients (57.6%, 95% CI: 41.07–74.09%) were assessed as having a partial response. The tumor regression grades (TRG) were, TRG1: 3 cases (9.1%, 95% CI: 1.90–25.97%), TRG2: 14 cases (42.4%, 95% CI: 26.27–60.38%), and TRG3: 2 cases (6.1%, 95% CI: 0.73–20.37%), respectively. Surgical safety reported as no cases of grade B/C anastomotic leakage or bowel obstruction. Adverse events (AEs) were manageable, with a 21.2% incidence of grade 3 events and no grade IV/V events or treatment‑related deaths. With a median follow‑up of 25.5 weeks, no recurrences were observed. Analysis of blood and tissue samples from patients with different treatment outcomes revealed significant activation of CD8+ T cells, NK cells, and M1 macrophage subsets in the tumor microenvironment of patients achieving pCR. These compelling data demonstrate promising efficacy with a favorable safety profile in MSS/pMMR LARC. These findings warrant studies to validate this regimen as a novel treatment paradigm for rectal cancer. ClinicalTrials.gov registration: NCT06108596.

sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: Colorectal cancer is the third most common cancer worldwide and the second leading cause of cancer-related death.1,2 In China, the incidence of rectal cancer has been rising in recent years, with low–mid rectal cancer and locally advanced rectal cancer (LARC) being particularly prominent.3,4

For patients with LARC, neoadjuvant radiotherapy or chemoradiotherapy has become the standard treatment modality; compared with adjuvant therapy, these approaches offer advantages in both oncological outcomes and quality of life.5 Immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs), particularly antibodies targeting programmed cell death protein 1 (PD-1) and its ligand programmed cell death ligand 1 (PD-L1), have demonstrated significant efficacy in various cancers, including colorectal cancers with high microsatellite instability (MSI-H) or deficient mismatch repair (dMMR).6,7 However, in LARC most patients exhibit microsatellite stable (MSS) or proficient mismatch repair (pMMR) status; thus, the efficacy of ICIs as monotherapy is limited. Such tumors are considered “cold tumors” due to insufficient immune infiltration.8

Recently, several studies have focused on combining radiotherapy to promote tumor antigen release and enhance immunogenicity, thereby improving the antitumor effects of ICIs and modestly increasing the pathological response rate after neoadjuvant treatment in LARC.9,10 Nonetheless, whether administered as short-course or long-course radiotherapy, the resultant radiation-induced injury, intestinal fibrosis, strictures, and impaired tissue healing remain significant challenges for subsequent surgical treatment and patient recovery.11,12

Previous studies have shown that preoperative total neoadjuvant chemotherapy (TNT) in LARC patients can achieve a disease-free survival (DFS) that is not inferior to that achieved with neoadjuvant chemoradiotherapy, with a pathological complete response (pCR) rate of up to 21.9% in surgically treated patients.13 In exploring strategies to convert “cold tumors” into “hot tumors,” numerous investigators have examined the immune microenvironment. They have developed novel methods to expose immunogenic tumor antigens, stimulate local inflammation within solid tumors, activate and recruit cross-presenting conventional dendritic cells (cDCs), maintain T-cell receptor (TCR) cytotoxicity or stem-like qualities, and preserve an appropriate linkage between the tumor microenvironment (TME) and draining lymph nodes—considered key to controlling tumor progression.14

In clinical practice, we have noted that the traditional antitumor agent interleukin‑2 (IL‑2) plays an important regulatory role in T‑cell activation.15 At both the cellular level and in animal models, combining a PD‑1 monoclonal antibody with IL‑2 has been shown to reprogram immunosuppressive tumor‑associated macrophages and enhance the diversity of the TCR repertoire, thereby driving CD8⁺ T cells toward a more effective state and improving antitumor efficacy.16 The antitumor effect of IL‑2 is closely linked to its dose; high doses can promote T‑cell proliferation and activation, induce a Th1‑type immune response, activate natural killer (NK) cell function, and stimulate the generation of lymphokine‑activated killer cells.17 These findings have encouraged us to explore a more effective and safe treatment strategy in LARC. Therefore, in this single‑arm PICS trial, our objective was to evaluate the efficacy and safety of combining ICIs and IL‑2 with total neoadjuvant chemotherapy in MSS/pMMR type LARC.

sec.title: Patient enrollment and baseline characteristics
sec.p: From November 2023 to December 2024, a total of 33 patients were screened and enrolled. Inter-rater agreement between radiologists and pathologists in image and slide interpretation exceeded 95% for all enrolled patients. All 33 patients received at least 4 cycles of neoadjuvant treatment with CapOX combined with sintilimab and IL‑2. Three patients discontinued further treatment for subjective reasons: one due to immunotherapy‑related pneumonitis, one due to immunotherapy‑related rash, and one due to severe vomiting. After evaluation, these patients exhibited significant tumor regression and proceeded to subsequent surgical treatment; they were included in the further analysis. The remaining 30 patients completed the prescribed 6 cycles of treatment and subsequently underwent radical surgery (Fig. 1). As shown in Table 1, the median age was 57.9 years (IQR 53.0–64.8), with 21 males (63.6%) and 12 females (36.4%). The ECOG performance status was 0 in 28 patients (84.8%) and 1 in 5 patients (15.2%). The tumor distance from the anal verge was ≤2 cm in 2 patients (6.1%), between 2 and 5 cm in 5 patients (15.2%), between 5 and 7 cm in 8 patients (24.2%) and between 7 and 12 cm (inclusive) in 18 patients (54.5%). Among these patients, T staging was T3 in 19 cases (57.6%), T4a in 11 cases (33.3%), and T4b in 3 cases (9.1%); N staging was N0 in 2 cases (6.1%), N1 in 9 cases (27.3%), and N2 in 22 cases (66.7%); positive CRM was observed in 22 cases (66.7%) and positive EMVI in 2 cases (6.1%). The median tumor mutational burden (TMB) was 4.1 Mutations/Mb (IQR 1.2–7.3), the median carcinoembryonic antigen (CEA) level was 5.7 ng/mL (IQR 2.1–12.7), and the median carbohydrate antigen 19‑9 (CA19‑9) level was 10.5 U/mL (IQR 6.3–24.2).

sec.title: Pathological and clinical treatment outcomes
sec.p: All 33 patients underwent subsequent radical surgery, with an average interval of 4.9 weeks (IQR 4.1–5.8) from the end of the last treatment to surgery. According to postoperative pathology, all 33 patients achieved R0 resection; among them, 14 patients (42.4%, 95% CI: 25.68–59.16%) achieved pCR, while the remaining 19 patients (57.6%, 95% CI: 41.07–74.09%) were assessed as having a partial response. Among the 14 pCR cases, 6 patients (18.2%, 95% CI: 5.02–31.34%) had been preoperatively assessed as having a clinical complete response (cCR). 19 patients (57.6%) were defined as major pathological response (MPR). According to AJCC standards, the tumor regression grading (TRG) scores of 1, 2, and 3 were observed in 3 cases (9.1%, 95% CI: 1.90–25.97%), 14 cases (42.4%, 95% CI: 26.27–60.38%), and 2 cases (6.1%, 95% CI: 0.73–20.37%), respectively. Postoperative T staging was as follows: T0 in 14 cases (42.4%), Tis in 1 case (3.0%), T1 in 2 cases (6.1%), T2 in 8 cases (24.3%), T3 in 7 cases (21.2%), and T4a in 1 case (3.0%). Postoperative N staging was N0 in 30 cases (90.9%), N1 in 1 case (3.0%), and N2 in 2 cases (6.1%). Overall postoperative TNM stages 0 to III were distributed as stage 0 in 14 cases (42.4%), stage I in 10 cases (30.3%), stage II in 6 cases (18.2%), and stage III in 3 cases (9.1%), as presented in Table 2.

sec.p: In addition, the median percentage change in the maximum tumor diameter on imaging compared with baseline was –60.7% (IQR –50% to –89%; Fig. 2). For the adjuvant therapy, all adjuvant treatments were developed based on postoperative pathology and MDT discussion. Among the 33 patients, 3 discontinued chemotherapy before surgery, 22 received two cycles of adjuvant therapy with CapOX combined with PD-1 inhibitors and IL-2 after surgery, 4 chose follow-up due to treatment intolerance, and another 4, who were assessed as having achieved pCR after surgery, also opted for follow-up without further treatment. Among the 14 patients who achieved pCR, 8 opted for a surveillance strategy (follow-up every 3 months including serum tumor markers, CT, and rectal MRI), while 6 received an additional 2 cycles of sintilimab + CapOX + IL-2. In the non-pCR group, 11 patients with Tis/T1/T2 disease and no lymph node metastasis received 2 additional cycles of sintilimab + CapOX + IL-2. For the 8 patients with T3/T4 disease or lymph node involvement, postoperative treatment included 2 cycles of the same regimen plus adjuvant radiotherapy.

sec.p: In the post-hoc analysis, as of the manuscript submission date, the median follow-up duration was 22.6 months (range: 17.7-27.4 months). During follow-up, one patient died due to severe respiratory failure (the patient had a pre-existing history of respiratory disease), and two patients experienced disease recurrence. Among the 33 patients who completed treatment and underwent surgery, the 1-year overall survival (OS) rate was 100% (95% CI: 89.4–100.0%), and the 1-year disease-free survival (DFS) rate was also 100% (95% CI: 89.4–100.0%). The 2-year OS rate was 97% (95% CI: 84.7–99.9%), and the 2-year DFS rate was 90.9% (95% CI: 75.7–97.1%) (Supplementary Fig. 1).

sec.title: Treatment-related adverse events and safety
sec.p: Of the 33 patients, 30 completed 6 cycles of neoadjuvant treatment, and adverse events (AEs) of any grade occurred in 31 patients (93.9%) (Table 3). The most common AE was vomiting, occurring in 31 patients (93.9%); followed by diarrhea in 13 patients (39.4%); myelosuppression in 10 patients (30.3%); hand–foot syndrome in 9 patients (27.3%); abnormal liver function in 6 patients (18.2%); and rash in 5 patients (15.2%). Among the patients who completed 6 cycles, 4 experienced grade 3 AEs-including 1 case of immunotherapy‑related hepatotoxicity, 2 cases of severe vomiting, and 1 case of myelosuppression. With active management, these patients were able to continue and complete subsequent neoadjuvant treatment and surgery. Overall, the incidence of grade 3 AEs was 7 out of 33 (21.2%), and no grade 4 or 5 AEs or treatment‑related deaths were observed.

sec.title: Surgical outcomes and safety
sec.p: Regarding surgical safety, among the 33 patients who underwent radical surgery, 30 underwent LAR and 3 underwent the Miles procedure; the postoperative mesorectal integrity rate was 29 cases (87.9%). One patient underwent Da Vinci robotic‑assisted surgery, while the remaining 32 patients underwent laparoscopic surgery. Two patients with severe diabetes and one patient with distal intestinal edema (postoperative pathological evaluation of ypT4aN1M0) underwent prophylactic terminal ileostomy; as of manuscript submission, all patients had completed ileostomy reversal. No cases of grade B/C anastomotic leakage or bowel obstruction were observed. One patient developed a postoperative abdominal incision infection (via a midline lower abdominal incision for mesorectal dissection, approximately 5–8 cm in length), one patient developed postoperative pneumonia that improved following aggressive anti‑infective treatment, and one patient developed postoperative intra‑abdominal infection due to severe diabetes, which improved with conservative treatment (Supplementary Table 1).

sec.title: Immune microenvironment changes during treatment
sec.p: We also collected specimens during neoadjuvant treatment, including blood and endoscopic biopsy tissues. We used flow cytometry to monitor changes in peripheral blood immune cell subsets to clarify the effects of PD-1 plus IL-2 on the immune environment. Additionally, multiplex immunofluorescence staining was performed to compare immune cell infiltration in the tumor microenvironment between pCR and non-pCR patients. As shown in Fig. 3a, immune cell subset distributions in pre-treatment blood samples were homogeneous with no significant differences between pCR and non-pCR groups. After four treatment cycles (Fig. 3b), the pCR group showed significant increases in the proportion of CD8+ T cells and the CD8/CD4 ratio, accompanied by increased NK cell subsets and M1 macrophage polarization. Correspondingly, tumor-killing cytokines such as IFN-γ, TNF-α, IL-6, and IL-1β were enriched in the blood. Furthermore, multiplex immunofluorescence of post-surgical tumor tissues (Fig. 3c) revealed significantly increased infiltration of CD8+ T cells, CD56+ NK cells, and CD68+ macrophages in tumors from pCR patients compared with non-pCR patients, suggesting notable immune cell activation and enrichment around the tumor site.

sec.title: Discussion
sec.p: In this phase II study, total neoadjuvant chemotherapy combined with a PD‑1 antibody and IL‑2 for mid–low LARC achieved a pCR rate of 42.4% and demonstrated favorable safety. This represents the first exploration of combining a traditional immunogenic antitumor agent with an ICI in the neoadjuvant treatment of MSS/pMMR type mid–low LARC. Moreover, the treatment regimen incorporated both a “subtraction” (omitting radiotherapy) and an “addition” (combining ICIs with IL‑2) approach to evaluate the efficacy and safety of this novel strategy in LARC.

A total of 33 patients were enrolled in this study, and no patients were excluded during the screening phase. Given the single-arm design and strict enrollment criteria, only patients confirmed to have MSS/pMMR mid–low LARC, with definitive histopathological diagnosis were included. During treatment, three patients did not complete the full six cycles of neoadjuvant therapy as protocol-specified; however, they all underwent subsequent surgical resection and achieved postoperative pathological results consistent with partial response. These patients were therefore retained in the final analysis without exclusion.

Currently, in MSS/pMMR mid–low LARC, reports have shown that PD‑1 antibody monotherapy is ineffective. Although combining chemoradiotherapy (either long‑ or short‑course) with synchronous or sequential PD‑1 therapy benefits some patients—with most studies using pCR as the primary endpoint and a few using the neoadjuvant rectal (NAR) score—the pCR rate in existing single‑arm studies ranges from 30% to 40%,18–20 and randomized controlled studies have reported rates between approximately 31.9% and 44.8%.21–25 Compared with these studies, the 42.4% pCR rate reported here is higher, suggesting that even without radiotherapy, the combination of a PD‑1 antibody with IL‑2 can yield significant clinical efficacy. However, further large‑sample, randomized controlled studies are necessary.

Furthermore, when comparing neoadjuvant chemotherapy alone, previous studies using the FOLFOX regimen (6 cycles) in LARC achieved a pCR rate of 21.9%. There is a paucity of reports on total neoadjuvant chemotherapy using the CapOX regimen, which may differ significantly from neoadjuvant chemoradiotherapy regarding treatment cycles. In addition, the French PRODIGE 23 multicenter randomized controlled trial demonstrated that, in patients with cT3 or cT4 M0 rectal cancer, administering six cycles of neoadjuvant FOLFIRINOX chemotherapy before preoperative chemoradiotherapy significantly improved treatment outcomes. Compared with preoperative chemoradiotherapy alone, this approach markedly increased disease-free survival and reduced neurotoxicity. In addition, TNT regimens incorporating chemoradiotherapy have improved pCR rates from the historical 15–20% to approximately 27–28%, as reported in landmark trials such as RAPIDO and PRODIGE 23 studies.26,27 Nevertheless, even within the TNT paradigm, the combination of chemotherapy and radiotherapy appears to have reached a plateau in terms of pCR achievement.26 In this study, the combination of the CapOX regimen with a PD‑1 antibody and IL‑2 raised the pCR rate to 42.4%, further confirming the synergistic effect of PD‑1 antibody and IL‑2. Although omitting radiotherapy raised concerns about local recurrence, the PROSPECT study13 provided sufficient confidence that, after omitting radiotherapy, a lower local recurrence rate could be achieved compared with the chemoradiotherapy group.

Regarding the combined use of IL‑2 and ICIs, although no reports have yet addressed this combination in LARC, the potential synergy between IL‑2 and PD‑1 has attracted considerable attention. Recently, a phase I clinical study of IBI363—a bispecific antibody fusion protein with a PD‑1/IL‑2α bias-in MSS/pMMR metastatic rectal cancer achieved an objective response rate of 13.6%,28 indirectly supporting the potential value of combining a PD‑1 antibody with IL‑2. In addition, dosing of IL‑2 has been a concern in the early phase of this study. Previous high‑dose regimens—administered either intravenously or subcutaneously—used a dose of 720,000 IU/kg per administration every 8 h, for up to 15 doses per cycle.29 In this study, a commercially available recombinant IL‑2 injection was used. In previous clinical antitumor treatments, we administered subcutaneous IL-2 concurrently with chemotherapy. Monitoring patients’ immune cell distributions revealed that after IL-2 injection, peripheral blood levels of CD8+ T cells, NK cells, and M1 macrophages showed a certain degree of increase. The evidence level for inferring whether the tumor has transitioned from a “cold” to a “hot” state based on peripheral blood mononuclear cell (PBMC) analysis is limited. Therefore, we also performed multiplex immunofluorescence staining on preoperative endoscopic biopsy tissues from patients to further evaluate the immunomodulatory sensitization effect of PD-1 antibody in combination with IL-2. This finding serves as one of the indirect evidence supporting the IL-2 regimen used in our current study. To ensure an effective blood concentration and avoid excessive toxicity, the dosing followed the antitumor treatment recommendations in the product label rather than the high‑dose regimens used in melanoma or metastatic renal cancer. Although this dose did not reach the high concentrations reported in previous studies, it was relatively higher than low‑dose regimens (72,000 IU/kg per administration).

Regarding postoperative treatment strategies, because non-randomized allocation may introduce confounding, postoperative management in this study was determined based on MDT consensus and patient preference. We acknowledge that the non-randomized nature of postoperative strategy (observation vs. continued treatment) precludes causal inference regarding recurrence outcomes—a key limitation inherent to single-arm trials. Nevertheless, although such postoperative management may introduce confounding effects on long-term outcomes such as overall survival (OS) or disease-free survival (DFS), the primary endpoint of this study—pCR rate—has already been achieved. Moreover, all patients achieved R0 resection according to postoperative pathology, which meets current guideline recommendations. The use of adjuvant radiotherapy in selected cases was intended to further reduce the risk of local recurrence. Importantly, this does not imply failure of radiation-sparing strategies; rather, in the majority of patients, we successfully avoided preoperative radiotherapy, thereby reducing radiation-related toxicities. Furthermore, adjuvant radiotherapy, when used as a salvage intervention, can effectively lower the risk of postoperative local recurrence. In future large-scale randomized controlled trials, we plan to further investigate salvage radiotherapy strategies tailored to postoperative pathological findings. We hope that the treatment paradigm established in this exploratory study—including the use of postoperative adjuvant radiotherapy—will ultimately yield favorable OS and DFS outcomes.

The study also revealed a clear discrepancy between the pCR rate and the cCR rate. In particular, 8 patients still showed significant tumor mass on imaging and endoscopy prior to surgery despite postoperative histopathology confirming no residual tumor cells. This observation offers new perspectives on preoperative cCR assessment criteria. Similar findings have been reported in studies such as NRG‑GI002.21 Because the primary endpoint of this study was pCR, all patients underwent radical resection rather than adopting a watch‑and‑wait strategy—even though one patient underwent the Miles procedure, with explicit informed consent obtained prior to enrollment. The discrepancy between cCR and pCR is not attributable to heterogeneity between preoperative imaging and postoperative pathological diagnosis. Rather, it primarily stems from the fact that many patients who achieved pCR still exhibited residual masses on preoperative imaging or endoscopic evaluation, despite negative tumor findings in endoscopic biopsies. Notably, the study protocol did not define a “near-cCR” endpoint. Consequently, all patients with visible residual masses proceeded to surgical resection, resulting in a lower number of cCR cases and a relatively higher pCR rate. In our ongoing randomized controlled trial (RCT), we have now integrated a response-adapted treatment algorithm: patients achieving cCR will enter a watch-and-wait program with maintenance immunotherapy, This approach aims to maximize functional outcomes while maintaining oncologic safety.

Omitting radiotherapy (“subtraction”) reduced its long‑term adverse effects on the intestine, bladder, and sexual function. Moreover, while surgery is typically scheduled 6–8 weeks after neoadjuvant chemoradiotherapy, the total neoadjuvant chemotherapy combined with PD‑1 + IL‑2 strategy shortened the interval from the last treatment to surgery. This reduction may help prevent tumor progression during the waiting period and lessen the risk of increased fibrosis, as the absence of radiotherapy decreases edema and fibrosis in the surgical area. Moreover, the CR rate of 42.4% under the premise of omitting radiotherapy still approaches the upper limit reported in previous studies, further supporting the advantages of this regimen. Regarding surgical quality, although 3 patients underwent the Miles procedure due to tumors located <2 cm from the anal verge, sphincter preservation was achieved in all other cases. No anastomotic leakage occurred—likely owing to the absence of additional radiation‑induced intestinal injury—even though 3 patients underwent prophylactic terminal ileostomy; postoperative imaging did not reveal any anastomotic leakage. With respect to drug‑related AEs, no treatment‑related deaths occurred among any patients in the PICS trial. Moreover, while severe (grade 3–4) treatment‑related AEs in neoadjuvant chemoradiotherapy combined or sequential with PD‑1 therapy have been reported at rates of 36%–48.2%, this study observed a rate of 21.2%. The overall AE incidence was 93.9%, which may be attributable to the 6 consecutive cycles of the CapOX regimen combined with IL‑2.

Limitations of the study include: (1) it is a small‑sample, open‑label, single‑arm phase II study with a relatively short follow‑up period; thus, although a high pCR rate was achieved, whether this translates into long‑term survival benefits requires longer follow‑up and more comprehensive evaluation; (2) radiotherapy is critical in preventing local recurrence in rectal cancer—especially in patients with high‑risk features—and although the PROSPECT study has provided evidence that total neoadjuvant chemotherapy can improve DFS, it remains to be determined whether the CapOX regimen used here can achieve outcomes comparable to the FOLFOX regimen; and (3) as a non‑randomized, open‑label trial, the study cannot be considered confirmatory, and further research is needed before these results can be generalized to a broader population of low rectal cancer patients; (4) Patient-reported outcomes (PROs) or quality of life (QOL) data were not incorporated in this study. However, based on the observed AE profile, low-grade vomiting (CTCAE Grade 1/2) occurred in patients (median duration: 1 day), predominantly within 24 h after chemotherapy. All episodes were managed with ondansetron and did not lead to treatment interruption. The symptom burden was clinically manageable. Although Grade 1/2 vomiting is commonly associated with oxaliplatin-based regimens, the addition of sintilimab and IL-2 in this regimen did not appear to significantly increase symptomatic burden. In future multicenter randomized controlled trials, PRO and QOL data will be prospectively collected and reported in greater detail; (5) this study was also limited by the high surgical expertise at the study center and the investigational IL-2 dosing regimen. However, the pCR endpoint is pathology-defined and therefore less susceptible to variability in surgical technique. The subcutaneous IL-2 regimen was intentionally designed to be safe and easily administrable to facilitate future multicenter implementation. Prior to broad clinical adoption, validation of this regimen in more diverse populations and healthcare settings will be necessary.

In summary, this study provides preliminary and encouraging results for patients with MSS/pMMR type LARC through the combination of total neoadjuvant chemotherapy with a PD‑1 antibody and IL‑2. The observed pCR rate of 42.4% represents a hypothesis-generating signal suggesting potential superiority over conventional therapy, which requires confirmation in future randomized controlled trials to establish clinical benefit. Besides, we also exhibited a controllable safety profile with no grade 4 or 5 AEs or treatment‑related deaths. Moreover, the innovative omission of radiotherapy reduced long‑term adverse effects on the intestine, bladder, and sexual function, and the shorter interval from the last treatment to surgery may contribute to a lower incidence of postoperative complications.

sec.title: Study design and inclusion criteria
sec.p: This single‑arm, open‑label trial was conducted at the Colorectal Cancer Center of the First Affiliated Hospital with Nanjing Medical University. The main inclusion criteria were as follows: patients aged 18 to 75 years with a pathological diagnosis of untreated rectal cancer, with the tumor located within 12 cm from the anal verge (inclusive), and with staging confirmed by contrast‑enhanced rectal magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) as either cT3/4N_anyM0 or cT_anyN⁺M0, with or without positive circumferential resection margin (CRM), extramural venous invasion (EMVI), or mesorectal fascia (MF) involvement. Staging was performed according to the 8th edition of the American Joint Committee on Cancer (AJCC) staging system. For molecular subtyping, rectal cancer cases were required to demonstrate stable expression of the mismatch repair proteins MLH1, MSH2, MSH6, and PMS2 via immunohistochemistry pMMR; and genomic DNA extracted from biopsy tissue had to be confirmed as MSS or low microsatellite instability (MSI‑L) by next‑generation sequencing and polymerase chain reaction (PCR). Both detection methods were required to be concordant. In the preoperative imaging assessment, a blinded evaluation method was adopted for diagnostic reporting. For each enrolled patient, imaging data were independently reviewed by two senior radiologists specialized in gastrointestinal oncology, and their reports were submitted to the leader of the colorectal tumor diagnosis team for final adjudication before an official radiological report was issued. Similarly, for pathological evaluation, two experienced pathologists independently conducted tissue sampling and slide preparation, each issuing their own pathology report. These reports were then reviewed by the leader of the colorectal tumor diagnosis team to reach a final pathological diagnosis. In addition, eligible patients needed an Eastern Cooperative Oncology Group (ECOG) performance status of 0–1 and normal hematologic, hepatic, and renal function to tolerate the trial. Exclusion criteria included: rectal cancer with distant metastases or staged as cTxNxM1, rectal cancers located more than 12 cm from the anal verge and colon cancers, MSI‑H or dMMR subtypes, previous exposure to immunotherapy/anticancer treatment, or a history of autoimmune diseases. Furthermore, to avoid confounding effects from other factors associated with high immune infiltration, patients with a TMB > 10 Mutations/Mb or POLE/POLD mutations were excluded.30 The complete list of inclusion and exclusion criteria is provided in the study protocol. All efficacy analyses followed the intention-to-treat principle. This study was conducted in accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki and was approved by the Ethics Committee of the First Affiliated Hospital of Nanjing Medical University (approval number 2023‑SR‑867). All patients provided written informed consent prior to enrollment.

sec.title: Study protocol
sec.p: After confirming eligibility, patients received treatment every three weeks according to the following regimen: on day 1 of treatment, patients received an intravenous infusion of oxaliplatin at 130 mg/m² and an intravenous infusion of sintilimab at 200 mg. This was followed by 14 consecutive days during which patients took oral capecitabine at 1250 mg/m² daily, along with subcutaneous injections of IL‑2 (1 million IU) administered every other day for a total of 7 injections. This was then followed by a 7‑day period without any antitumor treatment. Based on previous protocols, an evaluation was performed after 2 cycles to assess tumor regression; if tumor regression exceeded 20%, the treatment was considered effective and the regimen was continued. If tumor regression was ≤20% or if disease progression was observed, the patient was withdrawn from the study, and following discussion by the multidisciplinary team (MDT), additional treatments such as radiotherapy were considered. Evaluations were performed every 2 cycles until the completion of 6 cycles. If severe AEs occurred, and if evaluation revealed a partial response with eligibility for R0 resection, patients were allowed to undergo surgical treatment once the AEs were controlled.

Following completion of the treatment, all enrolled patients underwent total mesorectal excision (TME) 4 to 6 weeks after the last treatment. The surgical approach was not restricted to low anterior resection (LAR) or abdominoperineal resection (Miles procedure), and the surgery could be performed via laparoscopy or using the Da Vinci robotic system. Postoperative adjuvant treatment was determined by MDT discussions and could include observation, continued use of CapOX (capecitabine plus oxaliplatin), or CapOX combined with PD‑1 antibody and IL‑2. Postoperative follow‑up was scheduled every three months during the first year and every six months thereafter until 3 years or death, via regular outpatient visits and/or telephone.

sec.title: Assessments
sec.p: Prior to treatment, all enrolled patients underwent baseline assessments including colonoscopy, histological evaluation, and imaging studies (comprising contrast‑enhanced rectal MRI and contrast‑enhanced computed tomography [CT] of the chest, abdomen, and head). Tumor staging before and after treatment was independently reported by three specialized radiologists using standardized imaging protocols. Imaging assessments were performed after every 2 treatment cycles. Upon completion of treatment, evaluations included a digital rectal examination, colonoscopy with multiple biopsies, imaging studies, and necessary laboratory tests. All surgeons performing the operations were required to have independently completed over 100 laparoscopic or Da Vinci robotic rectal cancer resections. All surgical videos were uploaded to a database and independently reviewed by two surgeons with experience in at least 100 cases each.

sec.title: Study endpoints
sec.p: The primary endpoint was the pCR rate, defined as the proportion of cases in which no viable tumor cells were detected in the resected tumor and lymph nodes among all evaluable cases. Secondary endpoints included the clinical complete response (cCR) rate, assessed based on the following criteria: endoscopic findings showing no visible tumor or only scar‑like changes, erythematous ulceration, or smooth strictures, negative results on multiple‑site biopsies, MRI findings (including diffusion‑weighted imaging [DWI] or T2‑weighted imaging) demonstrating either a normal bowel wall or significant fibrosis at the original tumor site, a digital rectal examination that did not detect any tumor or ulceration. Other secondary endpoints included the R0 resection rate (the proportion of cases with negative microscopic margins), major pathological response (MPR; defined as ≤10% residual viable tumor cells in the tumor bed regardless of lymph node status), and tumor regression grading (TRG) determined according to the AJCC 8th edition guidelines (with TRG 0, 1, 2, and 3 representing no residual tumor cells, single or small clusters of cells, residual cancer with a fibrotic response, and minimal evidence of tumor response, respectively). In addition, 3‑year disease‑free survival (DFS; defined as the time from enrollment to first recurrence or death from any cause), rates of local and distant recurrence and 3‑year overall survival (OS; defined as the time from enrollment to death from any cause) were planned as survival endpoints; however, these data have not yet matured and will be reported later. Safety was also an observational endpoint and included AEs during neoadjuvant treatment and postoperative complications. All safety endpoints were assessed according to the Common Terminology Criteria for Adverse Events (CTCAE) version 5.0. During neoadjuvant treatment, AEs were monitored every two weeks, and their management followed the guidelines provided by the Society for Immunotherapy of Cancer (SITC) Toxicity Management Working Group.

sec.title: Statistical analysis
sec.p: The sample size was calculated based on the primary endpoint. Previous studies indicated that the pCR rate for neoadjuvant chemoradiotherapy in LARC is approximately 15–20%; accordingly, this study set p₀ at 15% and p₁ at 30%, with α = 0.05 and β = 0.20. Using Simon’s two‑stage design, the first stage planned to recruit 12 patients. If no response was observed among these 12 subjects, recruitment for this cohort would be terminated. If 3 or more responses were observed, the study would progress to the second stage, during which an additional 21 subjects would be recruited, for a total of 33. At the end of the second stage, if 7 or fewer responses were observed among the 33 subjects, further investigation would not be pursued. Continuous variables were expressed as mean ± interquartile range (IQR) and analyzed using an unpaired t‑test, while categorical variables were analyzed using the chi‑square test combined with Fisher’s exact test and expressed as counts and percentages. All tests were two‑sided, with a p‑value < 0.05 considered statistically significant. Categorical variables were analyzed using Fisher’s exact test due to small sample sizes and expected cell frequencies <5 in subgroups. Continuous variables were compared using the Mann-Whitney U test as normality assumptions were unmet. No adjustment for multiple comparisons was performed due to the exploratory nature of this phase II trial and the small sample size, which would reduce statistical power if stringent corrections (e.g., Bonferroni) were applied. Binomial confidence intervals for pCR rates were computed using the Clopper-Pearson method. To control the false discovery rate (FDR) arising from multiple testing across prespecified efficacy endpoints, p-values were adjusted using the Benjamini-Hochberg procedure, with an FDR threshold set at 0.1. Survival probabilities were estimated by use of the Kaplan-Meier method. Overall survival and disease-free survival along with 95% CIs were calculated (post-hoc analyses) by log-rank tests. Safety analyses were primarily descriptive; all AEs were summarized using frequency and percentage. As the safety analysis aimed to comprehensively characterize the toxicity profile rather than test specific hypotheses, no multiplicity adjustment was applied to safety endpoints. All statistical analyses were performed using R software (version 4.2.1).
